title: Big Four slash graduate jobs as AI takes over entry-level tasks
author: Scottish Financial News

dom.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks

mo.t: Big Four: Integration matters more than replacement
Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
Staffing structure: AI threatens both pyramid and pipeline
Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing

kp.k: Big Four reduced entry-level recruitment amid AI adoption
kp.d: The article reports that Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC are offering fewer positions to UK graduates and school leavers than in 2023. It attributes this contraction partly to growing reliance on AI for entry-level administrative tasks, while also identifying cost reduction, offshoring and the post-Covid consulting slowdown as contributing factors.
qs: The Big Four accountancy firms – Deloitte, EY, KPMG, and PwC – have significantly reduced job opportunities for new graduates and school leavers, while simultaneously cutting existing roles, as the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) increases.
With the growing reliance on AI to perform many entry-level administrative tasks, hundreds fewer graduates and school leavers will be recruited compared to 2023, The Telegraph reports.

kp.k: KPMG made the largest reported recruitment reduction
kp.d: KPMG's recruitment scheme fell 29%, from 1,399 hires in 2023 to 942 in 2024, with approximately 1,000 hires expected in 2025. The article presents this as the largest reduction among the four firms.
qs: KPMG has implemented the most significant cuts, slashing its recruitment scheme by 29% from 1,399 in 2023 to 942 last year, with around 1,000 expected hires this year.

kp.k: Other firms also contracted graduate hiring
kp.d: Deloitte reduced its graduate intake by 18%, EY by 11% and PwC by 6%. Deloitte expected recruitment to remain flat in 2025; the article supplies no equivalent 2025 forecast for EY or PwC.
qs: Deloitte followed suit with an 18% reduction in its graduate intake, from 1,700 to 1,400, and anticipates flat recruitment this year.
EY trimmed its graduate hiring by 11% (1,800 to 1,600), while PwC cut its entry-level scheme by 6% (1,600 to 1,500).

kp.k: Accountancy graduate adverts declined faster than wider listings
kp.d: Indeed data reportedly show that UK accountancy graduate job advertisements in 2025 were 44% below their 2023 level. The article compares this with a 33% decline across all graduate jobs and a 20% decline in general job listings.
qs: Data from job board Indeed has revealed a 44% decrease in UK accountancy graduate job adverts this year compared to 2023, notably higher than the 33% decline for all graduate jobs and a 20% drop in general job listings.

kp.k: Overall Big Four headcounts also fell
kp.d: Executive search firm Patrick Morgan is cited for reductions in total UK headcount following ChatGPT's November 2022 emergence. In 2025, KPMG and PwC were reportedly down 4%, Deloitte 2% and EY 1%; the article does not isolate how much of these reductions was caused by AI.
qs: Beyond graduate roles, executive search firm Patrick Morgan indicates that the Big Four have significantly reduced their overall UK headcounts since the emergence of ChatGPT in November 2022.
So far in 2025, KPMG and PwC have both seen a 4% reduction in their total UK headcounts.
Deloitte's UK workforce is down by 2% since last year, and EY's by 1%.

kp.k: Larger workforce cuts followed post-Covid consulting expansion
kp.d: The article reports sharper UK workforce reductions in 2024—7% at KPMG, 5% at both PwC and Deloitte, and 3% at EY—and situates them after a post-Covid consulting boom that had produced substantial workforce growth.
qs: Even sharper cuts were made in 2024, following a post-Covid boom in the consulting industry that led to significant workforce expansion.
KPMG reduced its UK workforce by 7% in 2024, PwC by 5%, Deloitte by 5%, and EY by 3%.

kp.k: AI and offshoring jointly support cost reduction
kp.d: The article characterises the cuts as part of a wider cost-reduction strategy involving both AI adoption and transferring work to lower-labour-cost countries. It identifies Malaysia, the Philippines and India and reports that the firms expanded operations in these locations during 2022 and 2023.
qs: The job cuts are part of a broader strategy to reduce costs, driven by the adoption of AI and the shifting of work to countries with lower labour costs, such as Malaysia, the Philippines, and India.
All four firms have also significantly expanded their operations in Malaysia and India in 2022 and 2023, with EY and PwC also expanding in the Philippines during the same period.

kp.k: Cost cutting affected partner payouts differently
kp.d: The article reports that Deloitte, PwC and EY experienced lower partner payouts during the slump, whereas KPMG avoided that trend through what the article calls aggressive cost-cutting measures.
qs: While Deloitte, PwC, and EY have experienced a decrease in partner payouts due to the slump, KPMG has managed to buck this trend by implementing aggressive cost-cutting measures.

kp.k: EY and KPMG maintained continued talent investment
kp.d: Despite reported reductions, EY and KPMG stated that they were continuing to recruit graduates, school leavers and apprentices. These are company statements about ongoing investment rather than evidence that prior intake levels will be restored; PwC and Deloitte declined to comment.
qs: Despite the cuts, EY and KPMG spokespersons affirmed their continued investment in talent, highlighting ongoing recruitment for their graduate, school leaver, and apprenticeship programmes.
EY said: "We are continuing to invest in talent across the UK and are actively hiring across all our graduate, school leaver and internship programmes."
KPMG said: "Investing in talent is important to us. We recruit around 1,000 graduates and apprentices a year."
PwC and Deloitte declined to comment.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Scottish Financial News reports that AI is taking over entry-level administrative tasks in accountancy and professional services, contributing to reduced graduate recruitment and wider workforce cuts at the Big Four.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain accountancy and professional-services source, not a claim about the Big Four's legal services. The article links increasing AI integration to fewer opportunities for graduates and school leavers and to reductions in existing roles. It presents AI adoption alongside offshoring as part of a cost-reduction strategy, while also describing a consulting slump after post-Covid expansion. Its forward-looking claim, attributed in the article to reporting by The Telegraph, is that hundreds fewer graduates and school leavers will be recruited in 2025 than in 2023.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article supports its account with recruitment figures, Indeed job-advert data and Patrick Morgan headcount estimates; it does not quantify the separate contribution of AI to the reductions.
pts.d: Reported intake figures are KPMG: 1,399 in 2023 to 942 in 2024, described as a 29% cut; Deloitte: 1,700 to 1,400, described as 18%; EY: 1,800 to 1,600, described as 11%; and PwC: 1,600 to 1,500, described as 6%. The KPMG percentage and counts are reproduced as reported, although they do not match arithmetically. Indeed supplies the comparison of accountancy graduate adverts with broader graduate and general job listings. Executive search firm Patrick Morgan is cited for overall UK headcount reductions: in 2025, 4% each at KPMG and PwC, 2% at Deloitte since the prior year and 1% at EY; in 2024, 7%, 5%, 5% and 3%, respectively. These are recruitment and workforce indicators rather than direct measurements of AI task substitution. The article also reports overseas expansion and cost-cutting but offers no task-level study or estimate isolating AI's effect from offshoring or the consulting downturn.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern reductions over 2023–2025, with near-term recruitment expectations for 2025 rather than a long-term forecast of wholesale job replacement.
pts.d: Published on 23 June 2025, the article compares recruitment with 2023, reports 2024 workforce cuts and describes reductions so far in 2025. It uses ChatGPT's November 2022 emergence as a reference point for headcount changes, not as a separately demonstrated causal mechanism. KPMG expects around 1,000 hires in 2025 and Deloitte expects flat recruitment. The account qualifies the AI narrative with post-Covid overexpansion, a consulting slump and offshoring. EY and KPMG spokespersons stress continued investment and recruitment, rather than an end to entry-level hiring.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are UK graduates, school leavers and existing Big Four employees; the broader context includes partners and overseas operations.
pts.d: Graduates and school leavers face fewer entry-level openings, particularly where administrative tasks can be performed by AI. Existing UK employees face wider headcount reductions, although the article does not identify which occupations account for those cuts or how many are directly attributable to AI. Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC are the provider organisations concerned. The article also reports lower partner payouts at Deloitte, PwC and EY due to the slump, with KPMG described as avoiding that trend through aggressive cost-cutting. Operations in Malaysia, India and the Philippines feature as destinations for lower-cost work and expansion. No specific effects on lawyers, legal clients or access to justice are asserted.
